screens.title: Branch Policies: Your Code's Gatekeepers
screens.narratorSegment: Branch policies in Azure Repos are a powerful set of rules that you can configure for specific branches, typically your main or develop branches, to ensure that all changes merged into them meet certain quality and compliance criteria. Think of them as automated gatekeepers. These policies are applied to Pull Requests, or PRs, targeting the protected branch, acting as a crucial checkpoint before a merge is allowed. This means no code can bypass these rules; every proposed change must satisfy the defined policies. For example, you might require that all code changes pass automated tests, receive a minimum number of peer reviews, or are linked to a specific work item in Azure Boards. By setting these policies, you're proactively preventing broken code, security vulnerabilities, or non-compliant changes from ever reaching your most stable branches, thereby maintaining the integrity and reliability of your entire codebase. It's about building quality in, not just checking for it at the end. How They Work

Applied to Pull Requests (PRs) targeting a protected branch, acting as gatekeepers before a merge is allowed.

screens.title: Minimum Reviewers: Collaborative Code Quality
screens.narratorSegment: One of the most common and vital branch policies is 'Require a minimum number of reviewers.' This policy ensures that at least a specified number of approved reviewers have thoroughly examined the code changes within a Pull Request. It's not just about catching bugs; it's also about fostering peer review, knowledge sharing, and maintaining consistent coding standards across the team. When configuring this policy, you'll set the minimum number of required approvals. For critical branches like main, a common practice is to require at least two reviewers. It's also crucial to disable the option 'Allow requestors to approve their own changes' for critical branches, as this would defeat the purpose of independent review. Additionally, you can enable 'Require approval from the last reviewer' to ensure that even after subsequent changes, the final version of the code has been re-approved. This policy significantly enhances code quality and reduces the risk of defects making their way into your stable branches. In practical terms, ensuring code changes are thoroughly vetted by peers before merging.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Minimum Reviewers: Collaborative Code Quality

Ensuring code changes are thoroughly vetted by peers before merging.

Policy Configuration
  • Minimum number of reviewers: Set to 2 or more for critical branches.
  • Allow requestors to approve their own changes: Generally disable for critical branches.
  • Require approval from the last reviewer: Enable for stricter control over final code.
Example Scenario

For the main branch, setting a minimum of two reviewers ensures that at least two sets of eyes, excluding the author's, validate the code before merging.

Key Takeaway

This policy is fundamental for peer review, knowledge sharing, and significantly reducing the risk of defects in your codebase.

screens.title: Automated Quality Gates: Build Validation
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond human review, automated quality checks are absolutely essential, and that's where 'Build validation' policies come into play. This policy requires that changes in a Pull Request successfully pass a specified Azure Pipeline build before the PR can be completed and merged. This is a critical safeguard that prevents broken code from ever reaching your protected branch. Imagine a scenario where a developer introduces a change that compiles locally but breaks the integration with other components, or causes existing tests to fail. Build validation catches these issues early, before they can destabilize your main or develop branch. You can configure which specific pipeline to run and whether the build must succeed for the policy to pass. This policy acts as an automated gatekeeper, ensuring that every merge maintains the integrity and functionality of your codebase, saving countless hours of debugging and preventing costly production issues down the line. A PR targeting main triggers a CI pipeline; if tests fail, the PR cannot be completed.

Build validation is a non-negotiable automated gate that ensures code quality and stability by enforcing successful builds before any merge.

screens.title: Extending Quality with Status Checks
screens.narratorSegment: To further extend your quality gates beyond just your build pipeline, Azure Repos offers the powerful policy of 'Require approval from external services,' often referred to as status checks. This policy allows you to integrate with a wide array of external tools and services, which then report a pass or fail status back to your Pull Request. The PR cannot be completed until all required external services report success. Imagine integrating a dedicated security scanner like SonarQube, a code quality analysis tool, or even custom scripts via webhooks that perform specific checks unique to your project. For instance, a security scanner might check for known vulnerabilities, and if any critical issues are found, it reports a 'fail' status, blocking the merge. This policy is incredibly flexible, allowing you to tailor your quality assurance process to include specialized checks that are vital for your application's security, performance, or compliance. It's about creating a comprehensive safety net that catches issues that a standard build might miss. screens.title: Traceability & Feedback: Linked Work Items and Comment Resolution
screens.narratorSegment: For robust project management and clear traceability, two additional branch policies are incredibly valuable: 'Require linked work items' and 'Check for comment resolution.' The 'Require linked work items' policy ensures that every code change is explicitly tied back to a specific task, bug, or feature in Azure Boards. This provides an invaluable audit trail, allowing you to easily trace why a change was made, what problem it solved, or what feature it implemented. It's crucial for understanding the context and impact of every commit. For example, if a bug is reported, you can quickly find the PR that fixed it and the associated work item. Complementing this, 'Check for comment resolution' ensures that all comments left during a Pull Request review are resolved before the PR can be merged. This prevents unaddressed feedback from being overlooked, ensuring that all concerns raised by reviewers are properly acknowledged and acted upon. Together, these policies enhance accountability, improve communication, and ensure that your codebase evolves in a structured and well-documented manner. screens.narratorSegment: In addition to branch policies, managing permissions within Azure Repos is absolutely critical for controlling who can do what. Module 2›Chapter 4›Permissions Hierarchy

Azure Repos Permissions: A Hierarchical Model

Understanding how permissions are inherited and applied across Azure DevOps.

Organization Level

Broadest permissions (e.g., create projects)

Project Level

Applies to all repos in a project (e.g., create repo)

Repository Level

Specific repo permissions (e.g., contribute, delete)

Branch Level

Most granular (e.g., force push, bypass policies)

Key Principle

Permissions are inherited from higher levels, but a 'Deny' at any level overrides an 'Allow' from a higher level.

Common Permissions
  • Read: View code.
  • Contribute: Push changes.
  • Bypass policies: Override branch policies.
  • Force push: Overwrite history.
Key Takeaway

Understanding the permission hierarchy is crucial for implementing precise access control, ensuring that team members have only the necessary privileges for their roles.

screens.title: Critical Permissions and Least Privilege
screens.narratorSegment: When managing permissions, it's vital to pay close attention to highly privileged actions, especially for protected branches. Permissions like 'Bypass policies when completing pull requests' and 'Force push' can undermine all your carefully configured branch policies. 'Force push,' for example, allows a user to overwrite the branch history, potentially deleting or altering commits from other team members. This can lead to significant data loss and confusion. Therefore, it's crucial to explicitly deny these highly privileged permissions for most developers, reserving them only for a select few, such as release managers or lead DevOps engineers, and only for emergency scenarios. This practice directly aligns with the 'Principle of Least Privilege,' or PoLP. PoLP states that users, programs, or processes should be granted only the minimum necessary privileges to perform their function. A common mistake is granting 'Project Administrator' roles too broadly, as this implicitly grants full control over all repositories and bypasses all policies. Always follow PoLP, granting only what's needed, and regularly review permissions as roles and project needs evolve to maintain a strong security posture. Critical Permissions and Least Privilege means the principle of least privilege dictates that users and groups should only receive the minimum permissions required for their role, preventing accidental or malicious actions like force pushes or policy bypasses on critical branches.. In practical terms, granting only the necessary permissions to prevent unauthorized actions.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Module 2›Chapter 4›Least Privilege

Critical Permissions and Least Privilege

Granting only the necessary permissions to prevent unauthorized actions.

High-Risk Permissions

  • Force push: Overwrites branch history, potentially losing work.
  • Bypass policies when completing PRs: Undermines all branch policies.
  • Delete repository: Irreversible data loss.

These should be explicitly Denied for most developers.

Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP)

Grant users, programs, or processes only the minimum necessary privileges to perform their function.

  • Reduces the attack surface and potential for damage.
  • Prevents accidental misuse of powerful permissions.
  • Enhances overall security posture.

Strictly adhering to the Principle of Least Privilege, especially for critical permissions, is fundamental to preventing unauthorized actions and maintaining a secure and stable codebase.
